input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_57
input_row.nl_statement:
\begin{itemize}
  \item[(a)] If either two columns or two rows of a square matrix are equal, then the determinant of the matrix equals 0.
  \item[(b)] Suppose \(A\) is a square matrix and \(B\) is the matrix obtained from \(A\) by swapping either two columns or two rows. Then \(\det A = -\det B\).
  \item[(c)] If one column or one row of a square matrix is multiplied by a scalar, then the value of the determinant is multiplied by the same scalar.
  \item[(d)] If a scalar multiple of one column of a square matrix is added to another column, then the value of the determinant is unchanged.
  \item[(e)] If a scalar multiple of one row of a square matrix is added to another row, then the value of the determinant is unchanged.
\end{itemize}
input_row.informal_proof:
All the assertions in this result follow from the result that the maps
\[
v_1, \dots, v_n \mapsto \det \left( \begin{array}{ccc} v_1 & \cdots & v_n \end{array} \right)
\quad \text{and} \quad
v_1, \dots, v_n \mapsto \det \left( \left( \begin{array}{ccc} v_1 & \cdots & v_n \end{array} \right)^t \right)
\]
are both alternating \(n\)-linear forms on \(\mathbb{F}^n\) [see 9.45 and 9.56(a)].

For example, to prove (d) suppose \(v_1, \dots, v_n \in \mathbb{F}^n\) and \(c \in \mathbb{F}\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\det\left( \begin{array}{cccc} v_1 + c v_2 & v_2 & \cdots & v_n \end{array} \right)
&= \det\left( \begin{array}{cccc} v_1 & v_2 & \cdots & v_n \end{array} \right)
+ c \det\left( \begin{array}{cccc} v_2 & v_2 & v_3 & \cdots & v_n \end{array} \right) \\
&= \det\left( \begin{array}{cccc} v_1 & v_2 & \cdots & v_n \end{array} \right),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first equation follows from the multilinearity property and the second equation follows from the alternating property. The equation above shows that adding a multiple of the second column to the first column does not change the value of the determinant. The same conclusion holds for any two columns. Thus (d) holds.

The proof of (e) follows from (d) and from 9.56(a). The proofs of (a), (b), and (c) use similar tools and are left to the reader.

input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_58
input_row.nl_statement: Suppose \(V\) is an inner product space and \(S \in \mathcal{L}(V)\) is a unitary operator. Then \(|\det S| = 1\).
input_row.informal_proof:
Because \(S\) is unitary, \(I = S^* S\) (see 7.53). Thus
\[
1 = \det(S^* S) = (\det S^*)(\det S) = \overline{\det S} \cdot \det S = |\det S|^2,
\]
where the second equality comes from 9.49(a) and the third equality comes from 9.56(c). The equation above implies that \(|\det S| = 1\).

input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_53
input_row.nl_statement:
Suppose \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\) and \(e_1, \dots, e_n\) is a basis of \(V\). Then
\[
\det T = \det \mathcal{M}(T, (e_1, \dots, e_n)).
\]
input_row.informal_proof:
Let \(f_1, \dots, f_n\) be the standard basis of \(\mathbb{F}^n\). Let \(S : \mathbb{F}^n \to V\) be the linear map such that \(S f_k = e_k\) for each \(k = 1, \dots, n\). Thus \(\mathcal{M}(S, (f_1, \dots, f_n), (e_1, \dots, e_n))\) and \(\mathcal{M}(S^{-1}, (e_1, \dots, e_n), (f_1, \dots, f_n))\) both equal the \(n \times n\) identity matrix. Hence

\[
\mathcal{M}(S^{-1} T S, (f_1, \dots, f_n)) = \mathcal{M}(T, (e_1, \dots, e_n)),
\]

as follows from two applications of 3.43. Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\det T &= \det(S^{-1} T S) \\
       &= \det \mathcal{M}(S^{-1} T S, (f_1, \dots, f_n)) \\
       &= \det \mathcal{M}(T, (e_1, \dots, e_n)),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the first line comes from 9.52, the second line comes from the definition of the determinant of a matrix, and the third line follows from 9.54.

input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_64
input_row.nl_statement: Suppose \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\) and \(q\) is the characteristic polynomial of \(T\). Then \(q(T) = 0\).
input_row.informal_proof:
If \(\mathbb{F} = \mathbb{C}\), then the equation \(q(T) = 0\) follows from 9.62 and 8.29.

Now suppose \(\mathbb{F} = \mathbb{R}\). Fix a basis of \(V\), and let \(A\) be the matrix of \(T\) with respect to this basis. Let \(S\) be the operator on \(\mathbb{C}^{\dim V}\) such that the matrix of \(S\) (with respect to the standard basis of \(\mathbb{C}^{\dim V}\)) is \(A\). For all \(z \in \mathbb{R}\) we have
\[
q(z) = \det(zI - T) = \det(zI - A) = \det(zI - S).
\]
Thus \(q\) is the characteristic polynomial of \(S\). The case \(\mathbb{F} = \mathbb{C}\) (first sentence of this proof) now implies that
\[
0 = q(S) = q(A) = q(T).
\]

input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_59
input_row.nl_statement:
Suppose \(V\) is an inner product space and \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\) is a positive operator. Then
\[
\det T \geq 0.
\]
input_row.informal_proof: By the spectral theorem (7.29 or 7.31), \(V\) has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of \(T\). Thus by the last bullet point of 9.42, \(\det T\) equals a product of the eigenvalues of \(T\), possibly with repetitions. Each eigenvalue of \(T\) is a nonnegative number (by 7.38). Thus we conclude that \(\det T \geq 0\).

input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_66
input_row.nl_statement:
Suppose \(A\) is an \(n \times n\) matrix. Let \(v_1, \dots, v_n\) denote the columns of \(A\). Then
\[
|\det A| \leq \prod_{k=1}^n \|v_k\|.
\]
input_row.informal_proof:
If \(A\) is not invertible, then \(\det A = 0\) and hence the desired inequality holds in this case.

Thus assume that \(A\) is invertible. The QR factorization (7.58) tells us that there exist a unitary matrix \(Q\) and an upper-triangular matrix \(R\) whose diagonal contains only positive numbers such that \(A = QR\). We have
\[
|\det A| = |\det Q||\det R|
= |\det R|
= \prod_{k=1}^n R_{k,k}
\leq \prod_{k=1}^n \|R_{*,k}\|
= \prod_{k=1}^n \|QR_{*,k}\|
= \prod_{k=1}^n \|v_k\|,
\]
where the first line comes from 9.49(b), the second line comes from 9.58, the third line comes from 9.48, and the fifth line holds because \(Q\) is an isometry.

input_row.nl_statement:
Suppose \(\mathbb{F} = \mathbb{C}\) and \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\). Let \(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_m\) denote the distinct eigenvalues of \(T\), and let \(d_1, \ldots, d_m\) denote their multiplicities. Then
\[
\det(zI - T) = (z - \lambda_1)^{d_1} \cdots (z - \lambda_m)^{d_m}.
\]
input_row.informal_proof: There exists a basis of \(V\) with respect to which \(T\) has an upper-triangular matrix with each \(\lambda_k\) appearing on the diagonal exactly \(d_k\) times (by 8.37). With respect to this basis, \(zI - T\) has an upper-triangular matrix with \(z - \lambda_k\) appearing on the diagonal exactly \(d_k\) times for each \(k\). Thus 9.48 gives the desired equation.

input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_67
input_row.informal_proof:
Let \(1, z, \dots, z^{n-1}\) be the standard basis of \(\mathcal{P}_{n-1}(\mathbb{F})\) and let \(e_1, \dots, e_n\) denote the standard basis of \(\mathbb{F}^n\). Define a linear map \(S: \mathcal{P}_{n-1}(\mathbb{F}) \to \mathbb{F}^n\) by
\[
Sp = \left(p(\beta_1), \dots, p(\beta_n)\right).
\]

Let \(A\) denote the Vandermonde matrix shown in the statement of this result. Note that
\[
A = \mathcal{M}(S, (1, z, \dots, z^{n-1}), (e_1, \dots, e_n)).
\]

Let \(T: \mathcal{P}_{n-1}(\mathbb{F}) \to \mathcal{P}_{n-1}(\mathbb{F})\) be the operator on \(\mathcal{P}_{n-1}(\mathbb{F})\) such that \(T1 = 1\) and
\[
T z^k = (z - \beta_1)(z - \beta_2)\cdots(z - \beta_k)
\quad \text{for } k = 1, \dots, n-1.
\]

Let
\[
B = \mathcal{M}(T, (1, z, \dots, z^{n-1}), (1, z, \dots, z^{n-1})).
\]
Then \(B\) is an upper-triangular matrix all of whose diagonal entries equal 1. Thus \(\det B = 1\) (by 9.48).

Let
\[
C = \mathcal{M}(ST, (1, z, \dots, z^{n-1}), (e_1, \dots, e_n)).
\]
Thus \(C = AB\) (by 3.81), which implies that
\[
\det A = (\det A)(\det B) = \det C.
\]

The definitions of \(C\), \(S\), and \(T\) show that \(C\) equals
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
1 & \beta_2 - \beta_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
1 & \beta_3 - \beta_1 & (\beta_3 - \beta_1)(\beta_3 - \beta_2) & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
1 & \beta_n - \beta_1 & (\beta_n - \beta_1)(\beta_n - \beta_2) & \cdots & (\beta_n - \beta_1)(\beta_n - \beta_2)\cdots(\beta_n - \beta_{n-1})
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Now \(\det A = \det C = \prod_{1 \leq j < k \leq n} (\beta_k - \beta_j)\), where we have used 9.56(a) and 9.48.

input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_70
input_row.nl_statement:
\[
\dim \mathcal{B}(V, W) = (\dim V)(\dim W).
\]
input_row.informal_proof:
Let \( e_1, \dots, e_m \) be a basis of \( V \) and \( f_1, \dots, f_n \) be a basis of \( W \). For a bilinear functional \( \beta \in \mathcal{B}(V, W) \), let \( \mathcal{M}(\beta) \) be the \( m \times n \) matrix whose entry in row \( j \), column \( k \) is \( \beta(e_j, f_k) \). The map \( \beta \mapsto \mathcal{M}(\beta) \) is a linear map of \( \mathcal{B}(V, W) \) into \( \mathbb{F}^{m,n} \).

For a matrix \( C \in \mathbb{F}^{m,n} \), define a bilinear functional \( \beta_C \) on \( V \times W \) by
\[
\beta_C(a_1 e_1 + \cdots + a_m e_m,\, b_1 f_1 + \cdots + b_n f_n)
= \sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^m C_{j,k} a_j b_k
\]
for \( a_1, \dots, a_m, b_1, \dots, b_n \in \mathbb{F} \).

The linear map \( \beta \mapsto \mathcal{M}(\beta) \) from \( \mathcal{B}(V, W) \) to \( \mathbb{F}^{m,n} \) and the linear map \( C \mapsto \beta_C \) from \( \mathbb{F}^{m,n} \) to \( \mathcal{B}(V, W) \) are inverses of each other because \( \beta_{\mathcal{M}(\beta)} = \beta \) for all \( \beta \in \mathcal{B}(V, W) \) and \( \mathcal{M}(\beta_C) = C \) for all \( C \in \mathbb{F}^{m,n} \), as you should verify.

Thus both maps are isomorphisms and the two spaces that they connect have the same dimension. Hence
\[
\dim \mathcal{B}(V, W) = \dim \mathbb{F}^{m,n} = mn = (\dim V)(\dim W).
\]

input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_56
input_row.nl_statement:
\begin{itemize}
  \item[(a)] Suppose \(A\) is a square matrix. Then \(\det A^t = \det A\).
  \item[(b)] Suppose \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\). Then \(\det T' = \det T\).
  \item[(c)] Suppose \(V\) is an inner product space and \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\). Then
  \[
  \det(T^*) = \overline{\det T}.
  \]
\end{itemize}
input_row.informal_proof:
(a) Let \(n\) be a positive integer. Define \(\alpha : (\mathbb{F}^n)^n \to \mathbb{F}\) by
\[
\alpha\left( \left( \begin{array}{ccc} v_1 & \cdots & v_n \end{array} \right) \right) = \det\left( \left( \begin{array}{ccc} v_1 & \cdots & v_n \end{array} \right)^t \right)
\]
for all \(v_1, \dots, v_n \in \mathbb{F}^n\). The formula in 9.46 for the determinant of a matrix shows that \(\alpha\) is an \(n\)-linear form on \(\mathbb{F}^n\).

Suppose \(v_1, \dots, v_n \in \mathbb{F}^n\) and \(v_j = v_k\) for some \(j \ne k\). If \(B\) is an \(n \times n\) matrix, then \(\left( \begin{array}{ccc} v_1 & \cdots & v_n \end{array} \right)^t B\) cannot equal the identity matrix because row \(j\) and row \(k\) of \(\left( \begin{array}{ccc} v_1 & \cdots & v_n \end{array} \right)^t B\) are equal. Thus \(\left( \begin{array}{ccc} v_1 & \cdots & v_n \end{array} \right)^t\) is not invertible, which implies that
\[
\alpha\left( \left( \begin{array}{ccc} v_1 & \cdots & v_n \end{array} \right) \right) = 0.
\]
Hence \(\alpha\) is an alternating \(n\)-linear form on \(\mathbb{F}^n\).

Note that \(\alpha\) applied to the standard basis of \(\mathbb{F}^n\) equals 1. Because the vector space of alternating \(n\)-linear forms on \(\mathbb{F}^n\) has dimension one (by 9.37), this implies that \(\alpha\) is the determinant function. Thus (a) holds.

(b) The equation \(\det T' = \det T\) follows from (a) and 9.53 and 3.132.

(c) Pick an orthonormal basis of \(V\). The matrix of \(T^*\) with respect to that basis is the conjugate transpose of the matrix of \(T\) with respect to that basis (by 7.9). Thus 9.53, 9.46, and (a) imply that
\[
\det(T^*) = \overline{\det T}.
\]

input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_60
input_row.nl_statement:
Suppose \(V\) is an inner product space and \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\). Then
\[
|\det T| = \sqrt{\det(T^*T)} = \text{product of singular values of } T.
\]
input_row.informal_proof:
We have
\[
|\det T|^2 = \overline{(\det T)}(\det T) = \left(\det(T^*)\right)(\det T) = \det(T^*T),
\]
where the middle equality comes from 9.56(c) and the last equality comes from 9.49(a). Taking square roots of both sides of the equation above shows that
\[
|\det T| = \sqrt{\det(T^*T)}.
\]

Let \(s_1, \ldots, s_n\) denote the list of singular values of \(T\). Thus \(s_1^2, \ldots, s_n^2\) is the list of eigenvalues of \(T^*T\) (with appropriate repetitions), corresponding to an orthonormal basis of \(V\) consisting of eigenvectors of \(T^*T\). Hence the last bullet point of 9.42 implies that
\[
\det(T^*T) = s_1^2 \cdots s_n^2.
\]
Thus \(|\det T| = s_1 \cdots s_n\), as desired.

input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_73
input_row.nl_statement:
Suppose \( v, v_1, v_2 \in V \) and \( w, w_1, w_2 \in W \) and \( \lambda \in \mathbb{F} \). Then
\[
(v_1 + v_2) \otimes w = v_1 \otimes w + v_2 \otimes w \quad \text{and} \quad v \otimes (w_1 + w_2) = v \otimes w_1 + v \otimes w_2
\]
and
\[
\lambda (v \otimes w) = (\lambda v) \otimes w = v \otimes (\lambda w).
\]
input_row.informal_proof:
Suppose \( (\varphi, \tau) \in V' \times W' \). Then
\begin{align*}
((v_1 + v_2) \otimes w)(\varphi, \tau) 
&= \varphi(v_1 + v_2) \, \tau(w) \\
&= \varphi(v_1) \, \tau(w) + \varphi(v_2) \, \tau(w) \\
&= (v_1 \otimes w)(\varphi, \tau) + (v_2 \otimes w)(\varphi, \tau) \\
&= (v_1 \otimes w + v_2 \otimes w)(\varphi, \tau).
\end{align*}

Thus \( (v_1 + v_2) \otimes w = v_1 \otimes w + v_2 \otimes w \).

The other two equalities are proved similarly.

input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_79
input_row.nl_statement:
Suppose \( U \) is a vector space.

(a) Suppose \( \Gamma \colon V \times W \to U \) is a bilinear map. Then there exists a unique linear map \( \widehat{\Gamma} \colon V \otimes W \to U \) such that
\[
\widehat{\Gamma}(v \otimes w) = \Gamma(v, w)
\]
for all \( (v, w) \in V \times W \).

(b) Conversely, suppose \( T \colon V \otimes W \to U \) is a linear map. Then there exists a unique bilinear map \( T^\# \colon V \times W \to U \) such that
\[
T^\#(v, w) = T(v \otimes w)
\]
for all \( (v, w) \in V \times W \).
input_row.informal_proof:
Let \( e_1, \ldots, e_m \) be a basis of \( V \) and let \( f_1, \ldots, f_n \) be a basis of \( W \). By the linear map lemma (3.4) and 9.74(b), there exists a unique linear map \( \widehat{\Gamma} \colon V \otimes W \to U \) such that
\[
\widehat{\Gamma}(e_j \otimes f_k) = \Gamma(e_j, f_k)
\]
for all \( j \in \{1, \ldots, m\} \) and \( k \in \{1, \ldots, n\} \).

Now suppose \( (v, w) \in V \times W \). There exist \( a_1, \ldots, a_m, b_1, \ldots, b_n \in \mathbb{F} \) such that
\[
v = a_1 e_1 + \cdots + a_m e_m \quad \text{and} \quad w = b_1 f_1 + \cdots + b_n f_n.
\]
Thus
\begin{align*}
\widehat{\Gamma}(v \otimes w)
&= \widehat{\Gamma} \left( \sum_{k = 1}^{n} \sum_{j = 1}^{m} (a_j b_k)(e_j \otimes f_k) \right) \\
&= \sum_{k = 1}^{n} \sum_{j = 1}^{m} a_j b_k \widehat{\Gamma}(e_j \otimes f_k) \\
&= \sum_{k = 1}^{n} \sum_{j = 1}^{m} a_j b_k \Gamma(e_j, f_k) \\
&= \Gamma(v, w),
\end{align*}
as desired, where the second line holds because \( \widehat{\Gamma} \) is linear, the third line holds by the definition of \( \widehat{\Gamma} \), and the fourth line holds because \( \Gamma \) is bilinear.

The uniqueness of the linear map \( \widehat{\Gamma} \) satisfying \( \widehat{\Gamma}(v \otimes w) = \Gamma(v, w) \) follows from 9.74(b), completing the proof of (a).

To prove (b), define a function \( T^\# \colon V \times W \to U \) by \( T^\#(v, w) = T(v \otimes w) \) for all \( (v, w) \in V \times W \). The bilinearity of the tensor product (see 9.73) and the linearity of \( T \) imply that \( T^\# \) is bilinear.

Clearly the choice of \( T^\# \) that satisfies the conditions is unique.

\[
\{ e_j \otimes f_k \}_{j = 1, \ldots, m;\, k = 1, \ldots, n}
\]
is a basis of \( V \otimes W \).

input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_80
input_row.nl_statement:
Suppose \( V \) and \( W \) are inner product spaces. Then there is a unique inner product on \( V \otimes W \) such that
\[
\langle v \otimes w, u \otimes x \rangle = \langle v, u \rangle \langle w, x \rangle
\]
for all \( v, u \in V \) and \( w, x \in W \).
input_row.informal_proof:
Suppose \( e_1, \ldots, e_m \) is an orthonormal basis of \( V \) and \( f_1, \ldots, f_n \) is an orthonormal basis of \( W \). Define an inner product on \( V \otimes W \) by
\begin{equation}
\left\langle \sum_{k=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{m} b_{j,k} \, e_j \otimes f_k, \sum_{k=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{m} c_{j,k} \, e_j \otimes f_k \right\rangle 
= \sum_{k=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{m} b_{j,k} \overline{c_{j,k}}.
\tag{9.81}
\end{equation}

The straightforward verification that (9.81) defines an inner product on \( V \otimes W \) is left to the reader [use 9.74(b)].

Suppose that \( v, u \in V \) and \( w, x \in W \). Let \( v_1, \ldots, v_m \in \mathbb{F} \) be such that 
\[
v = v_1 e_1 + \cdots + v_m e_m,
\]
with similar expressions for \( u, w, \) and \( x \). Then
\begin{align*}
\langle v \otimes w, u \otimes x \rangle 
&= \left\langle \sum_{j=1}^{m} v_j e_j \otimes \sum_{k=1}^{n} w_k f_k, \sum_{j=1}^{m} u_j e_j \otimes \sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k f_k \right\rangle \\
&= \left\langle \sum_{k=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{m} v_j w_k \, e_j \otimes f_k, 
\sum_{k=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{m} u_j x_k \, e_j \otimes f_k \right\rangle \\
&= \sum_{k=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{m} v_j \overline{u_j} \, w_k \overline{x_k} \\
&= \left( \sum_{j=1}^{m} v_j \overline{u_j} \right)
   \left( \sum_{k=1}^{n} w_k \overline{x_k} \right) \\
&= \langle v, u \rangle \langle w, x \rangle.
\end{align*}

There is only one inner product on \( V \otimes W \) such that 
\[
\langle v \otimes w, u \otimes x \rangle = \langle v, u \rangle \langle w, x \rangle
\]
for all \( v, u \in V \) and \( w, x \in W \) because every element of \( V \otimes W \) can be written as a linear combination of elements of the form \( v \otimes w \) [by 9.74(b)].

input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_83
input_row.nl_statement:
Suppose \( V \) and \( W \) are inner product spaces, and \( e_1, \ldots, e_m \) is an orthonormal basis of \( V \) and \( f_1, \ldots, f_n \) is an orthonormal basis of \( W \). Then
\[
\{ e_j \otimes f_k \}_{j=1,\ldots,m;\,k=1,\ldots,n}
\]
is an orthonormal basis of \( V \otimes W \).
input_row.informal_proof:
We know that 
\[
\{ e_j \otimes f_k \}_{j=1,\ldots,m;\,k=1,\ldots,n}
\]
is a basis of \( V \otimes W \) [by 9.74(b)]. Thus we only need to verify orthonormality.

To do this, suppose \( j, M \in \{1, \ldots, m\} \) and \( k, N \in \{1, \ldots, n\} \). Then
\[
\langle e_j \otimes f_k, e_M \otimes f_N \rangle 
= \langle e_j, e_M \rangle \langle f_k, f_N \rangle 
= \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } j = M \text{ and } k = N, \\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

Hence the doubly indexed list 
\[
\{ e_j \otimes f_k \}_{j=1,\ldots,m;\,k=1,\ldots,n}
\]
is indeed an orthonormal basis of \( V \otimes W \).

input_row.name: LADR_thm_chap_9_65
input_row.nl_statement:
Suppose \(T \in \mathcal{L}(V)\). Let \(n = \dim V\). Then the characteristic polynomial of \(T\) can be written as
\[
z^n - (\operatorname{tr} T) z^{n-1} + \cdots + (-1)^n (\det T).
\]
input_row.informal_proof:
The constant term of a polynomial function of \(z\) is the value of the polynomial when \(z = 0\). Thus the constant term of the characteristic polynomial of \(T\) equals \(\det(-T)\), which equals \((-1)^n \det T\) (by the third bullet point of 9.42).

Fix a basis of \(V\), and let \(A\) be the matrix of \(T\) with respect to this basis. The matrix of \(zI - T\) with respect to this basis is \(zI - A\). The term coming from the identity permutation \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) in the formula 9.46 for \(\det(zI - A)\) is
\[
(z - A_{1,1}) \cdots (z - A_{n,n}).
\]
The coefficient of \(z^{n-1}\) in the expression above is \(-(A_{1,1} + \cdots + A_{n,n})\), which equals \(-\operatorname{tr} T\). The terms in the formula for \(\det(zI - A)\) coming from other elements of \(\text{perm } n\) contain at most \(n - 2\) factors of the form \(z - A_{k,k}\) and thus do not contribute to the coefficient of \(z^{n-1}\) in the characteristic polynomial of \(T\).
